textbookText: Anders Celsius (27 November 1701 – 25 April 1744) was a Swedish astronomer, physicist and mathematician. He was professor of astronomy at Uppsala University from 1730 to 1744, but traveled from 1732 to 1735 visiting notable observatories in Germany, Italy and France. He founded the Uppsala Astronomical Observatory in 1741, and in 1742 proposed (an inverted form of) the Centigrade temperature scale which was later renamed Celsius in his honour.

[Fig.9.2] 9.1 Introduction Heat and temperature have a great influence on the behavior of matter and the world around us. They have a fundamental role in all events from the everyday experience of feeling warmth from the sun to the complex processes of thermal equilibrium and heat transfer in various systems. Heat and temperature are closely related. Heat refers to the transfer of thermal energy between systems as a result of temperature difference whereas temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of molecules within a system. In this chapter, we study the definitions, properties, and applications of thermal energy, heat, and temperature to dig out their mysteries. 9.2 Thermal Energy Thermal energy is the most basic form of energy contained within a system or an atom. Thermal energy is not in transit but remains stored in the system as its kinetic energy. Thermal energy is responsible for random movements of the molecules, or atoms, and that makes the atoms and molecules move faster. Thermal energy gives the total kinetic energy possessed by a system. Therefore, the thermal energy of a body is responsible for its temperature. In a system, it increases with an increase in temperature and hence it is used to determine the internal energy of such a system. Internal energy includes the kinetic energy and potential energy of molecules within a substance. The kinetic energy component of internal energy is directly related to the thermal energy of the system. Thermal energy has been used for heating, boiling water and cooking food , etc. since the beginning of the human race. From the beginning, the primary sources of the thermal energy were the sun and fire, but technological evolution over the years has expanded the scope to new man-made energy sources such as geothermal energy, nuclear heat, waste heat, and electrical energy. Chemical energy and wind energy are other sources of thermal energy used throughout. Observations reveal that a hot object possesses a considerable amount of thermal energy, while a cold object has a smaller amount. This concept can be illustrated by a common experience: rubbing our hands together on a freezing winter day. In this scenario, the kinetic energy of our hands is transformed into thermal energy through the friction generated between them. When a substance is heated, its temperature increases because the average kinetic energy of the molecules increases. At a higher temperature, molecules have greater kinetic energy and move more rapidly. This increased motion leads to more frequent and energetic collisions between molecules. Consequently, thermal energy is transferred from the higher temperature region to the lower temperature. This transfer of thermal energy is known as heat. 9.3 Heat When we place a hot object in thermal contact with a cold object, the thermal energy gets transferred from the hot object into the cold one until they attain thermal equilibrium. This thermal energy in transit is commonly referred to as heat. Hence, heat energy is the transfer of thermal energy between two objects at different temperatures. Heat, being a form of energy, is not a physical object; therefore, we cannot sense it by merely looking at an object, but rather feel it when we touch it. The Sun stands out as a significant and natural source of heat energy. In contemporary times, the heat energy, we primarily use is derived from natural sources like gas and oil.
